interactions.label: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is a unique exception in the classification

params.question: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is a unique exception in the classification of haemolytic anaemias because it is:

answers.text: A hereditary condition with an extracorpuscular defect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. PNH is an acquired disorder caused by a somatic PIG-A gene mutation, not an inherited one.

answers.text: An acquired condition with an intracorpuscular defect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. PNH arises from a somatic PIG-A mutation within the haematopoietic stem cell, making the defect intracorpuscular. Yet it is acquired, not inherited — the only haemolytic anaemia that breaks the general rule that intracorpuscular defects are hereditary.

answers.text: A hereditary condition that causes intravascular haemolysis only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. PNH is acquired, not hereditary. While it does cause intravascular haemolysis, its uniqueness lies in being acquired yet intracorpuscular.

answers.text: An acquired condition with an extracorpuscular defect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Most acquired haemolytic anaemias are extracorpuscular, but PNH is the exception — its defect (loss of CD55 and CD59) sits within the red cell itself.

overallFeedback.feedback: PNH is unique because it breaks the general rule: nearly all intracorpuscular defects are hereditary, but PNH is acquired. The somatic PIG-A mutation removes complement regulators from the cell surface — an intrinsic defect that is not inherited.
Exactly right. PNH is the sole acquired intracorpuscular haemolytic anaemia, breaking the general rule that intracorpuscular defects are hereditary.

interactions.label: In haemolytic anaemia, the jaundice produces dark-coloured urine and pale stools

params.question: In haemolytic anaemia, the jaundice produces dark-coloured urine and pale stools.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Haemolytic jaundice is acholuric. The unconjugated bilirubin produced by red cell destruction is not water-soluble and cannot pass into the urine. Both urine and stool colour remain normal. Dark urine and pale stools point to obstructive jaundice, where conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Haemolytic jaundice is acholuric — the excess unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and protein-bound, so it cannot be filtered by the kidneys. Urine and stool colour remain normal. Dark urine with pale stools is the hallmark of obstructive jaundice.

interactions.label: In sickle cell disease, Howell-Jolly bodies appear on the peripheral blood smear

params.question: In sickle cell disease, Howell-Jolly bodies appear on the peripheral blood smear because:

answers.text: Haemoglobin S polymer damages the red cell nucleus directly

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Mature red cells are anucleate. Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants that a functional spleen would normally remove, not a result of direct nuclear damage.

answers.text: Repeated splenic infarctions render the patient functionally asplenic

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In sickle cell disease, sickled red cells repeatedly infarct the spleen, progressively destroying it by late childhood. Without a functioning spleen, nuclear remnants (Howell-Jolly bodies) persist in circulating red cells.

answers.text: Bone marrow stress releases nucleated red cells prematurely

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Nucleated red cells may be released under marrow stress, but Howell-Jolly bodies are small nuclear remnants in mature cells that persist because the spleen can no longer remove them.

answers.text: Iron overload from chronic transfusions impairs splenic macrophage function

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While transfusional iron overload can occur, Howell-Jolly bodies in sickle cell disease result from progressive autosplenectomy due to repeated splenic infarctions, not iron toxicity.

overallFeedback.feedback: Howell-Jolly bodies appear because the spleen, which normally removes nuclear remnants, is progressively destroyed by repeated sickling-induced infarctions — a process called autosplenectomy.
Well done. Autosplenectomy from repeated infarctions is a hallmark of sickle cell disease. Howell-Jolly bodies are the smear evidence that the spleen is no longer functional.

interactions.label: In beta-thalassaemia major, the predominant mechanism of anaemia is:

params.question: In beta-thalassaemia major, the predominant mechanism of anaemia is:

answers.text: Peripheral destruction of red cells by splenic macrophages

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While some peripheral destruction occurs, the predominant mechanism is ineffective erythropoiesis — destruction of red cell precursors within the marrow itself, before they are released.

answers.text: Autoimmune-mediated red cell lysis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Thalassaemia is a genetic disorder of globin chain production, not an autoimmune process. The anaemia results from imbalanced globin chains damaging precursors in the marrow.

answers.text: Precipitation of excess unpaired alpha chains destroying erythroid precursors in the marrow

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In beta-thalassaemia major, absent or reduced beta chains leave excess alpha chains that precipitate as inclusion bodies within developing erythroid precursors. This intramedullary destruction is called ineffective erythropoiesis and is the primary cause of anaemia.

answers.text: Reduced iron absorption leading to inadequate haemoglobin synthesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Iron absorption is actually increased in thalassaemia due to suppressed hepcidin. The anaemia is caused by destruction of red cell precursors from precipitated excess alpha chains, not iron deficiency.

overallFeedback.feedback: In beta-thalassaemia major, excess unpaired alpha chains precipitate as inclusion bodies within erythroid precursors in the bone marrow, destroying them before they mature. This process — ineffective erythropoiesis — is the primary mechanism, unlike sickle cell disease where destruction is peripheral.

Exactly right. Ineffective erythropoiesis — intramedullary destruction of precursors by precipitated alpha chain inclusions — distinguishes beta-thalassaemia from sickle cell disease, where haemolysis is peripheral.

interactions.label: In cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, the direct antiglobulin test (Coombs test

params.question: In cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, the direct antiglobulin test (Coombs test) typically shows:

answers.text: IgG positive, C3d negative

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. This pattern indicates warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, where IgG antibodies bind red cells at body temperature. In cold AIHA, IgM is the pathogenic antibody.

answers.text: IgG negative, C3d positive

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In cold AIHA, IgM antibodies bind red cells in the cool periphery and activate complement, depositing C3d. When blood returns to body temperature, IgM dissociates but C3d remains on the cell surface. The DAT therefore detects complement but not immunoglobulin.

answers.text: Both IgG and C3d positive

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A dual-positive result suggests mixed-type autoimmune haemolytic anaemia. Pure cold AIHA shows C3d positivity only because the IgM antibody dissociates at body temperature.

answers.text: Both IgG and C3d negative

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A completely negative DAT points toward non-immune causes of haemolysis. Cold AIHA does leave a complement footprint — C3d — on the red cell surface.

overallFeedback.feedback: In cold AIHA, IgM binds at low temperatures and activates complement (C3d) on red cells. At 37°C, IgM dissociates but C3d stays. The DAT therefore shows C3d positive with IgG negative — distinguishing it from warm AIHA, which shows IgG positive.

Well done. The key insight is that IgM binds red cells only in the cold periphery and detaches at body temperature, but the complement it activates (C3d) remains fixed — giving the characteristic C3d-only pattern.

interactions.label: In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, the pathological mechanism that drives r

params.question: In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, the pathological mechanism that drives red cell fragmentation is:

answers.text: Shiga toxin–mediated endothelial injury in glomerular capillaries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Shiga toxin–mediated endothelial damage is the mechanism in haemolytic uraemic syndrome, not TTP. Both produce schistocytes, but the underlying defect differs.

answers.text: Deficiency of ADAMTS13 allowing ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers to persist and seed platelet microthrombi

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ADAMTS13 normally cleaves ultra-large VWF multimers. When deficient, these multimers persist and cause platelet microthrombi throughout the microvasculature. Red cells shearing against these fibrin-platelet strands fragment into schistocytes.

answers.text: Somatic PIG-A mutation removing complement regulators from the red cell membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Loss of complement regulators CD55 and CD59 from a PIG-A mutation describes paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, not TTP.

answers.text: Direct parasitic invasion and rupture of red blood cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Direct parasitic destruction of red cells describes malaria, particularly falciparum infection. TTP involves mechanical fragmentation of red cells by microthrombi, not infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: In TTP, ADAMTS13 deficiency lets ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers persist in the circulation. These seed platelet microthrombi that mechanically shear red cells into schistocytes. This is a haematological emergency requiring urgent plasmapheresis.

Exactly right. ADAMTS13 deficiency is the central defect in TTP. Urgent plasmapheresis to replace ADAMTS13 and remove the ultra-large multimers is the treatment — making this a haematological emergency.

interactions.label: A patient with confirmed haemolysis has spherocytes on the peripheral blood smea

params.question: A patient with confirmed haemolysis has spherocytes on the peripheral blood smear and a negative direct antiglobulin test. The most likely diagnosis is:

answers.text: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Warm AIHA does produce spherocytes, but the direct antiglobulin test would be positive for IgG. A negative DAT with spherocytes points to an intrinsic membrane defect.

answers.text: Cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Cold AIHA shows red cell agglutination on the smear, not isolated spherocytes. The DAT would also show C3d positivity.

answers.text: Hereditary spherocytosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The diagnostic algorithm directs: spherocytes on the smear → perform DAT. A positive DAT confirms warm AIHA; a negative DAT points to hereditary spherocytosis, where an intrinsic membrane protein defect (spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3) produces spherocytes without immune coating.

answers.text: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. MAHA produces schistocytes (fragmented helmet-shaped cells), not spherocytes. The morphological pattern on the smear is the first triage step in the diagnostic algorithm.

overallFeedback.feedback: The algorithm teaches: spherocytes → DAT. DAT positive = warm AIHA. DAT negative = hereditary spherocytosis. The membrane protein defect in hereditary spherocytosis produces spherocytes independently of any immune mechanism.
Well done. You applied the three-step algorithm correctly: confirm haemolysis, read the smear morphology, then use the DAT to distinguish immune from non-immune causes.
